acceptedAnswer.text: Inheritance in Java is an OOP mechanism where one class (subclass/child) acquires the fields and methods of another class (superclass/parent) using the 'extends' keyword. It models the IS-A relationship — a Dog IS-A Animal. Inheritance promotes code reuse: common behaviour defined once in the parent is automatically available in all subclasses. Java supports single inheritance for classes (one direct parent) but a class can implement multiple interfaces.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between method overriding and method overloading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Method Overriding: subclass provides a new implementation for a method already defined in the parent class. Same name, same parameter list, same or covariant return type. Resolved at RUNTIME (dynamic dispatch). Requires inheritance. Method Overloading: same class defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists. Resolved at COMPILE TIME. Does not require inheritance. Overriding = runtime polymorphism. Overloading = compile-time polymorphism.

mainEntity.name: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance through classes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java avoids the 'Diamond Problem' — if class C extends both A and B, and both A and B override the same method from a common ancestor, which version does C inherit? This ambiguity makes the language complex and error-prone. Java solves this by: (1) Allowing only single inheritance for classes. (2) Allowing multiple interface implementation — interfaces define contracts without concrete state, so no diamond ambiguity. Java 8+ default methods in interfaces can create a similar conflict, resolved by explicit override rules.

mainEntity.name: What is the super keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 'super' keyword in Java refers to the immediate parent class. Three uses: (1) 'super.field' — access a parent field hidden by a subclass field with the same name. (2) 'super.method()' — call the parent's version of an overridden method. (3) 'super(args)' — call the parent's constructor from the subclass constructor; must be the first statement. If no explicit super() is written in a subclass constructor, Java auto-inserts 'super()' (no-arg parent constructor).

mainEntity.name: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that objects of a subclass must be substitutable for objects of the parent class without altering the correctness of the program. In simple terms: wherever a Parent type is expected, a Child object must work correctly. Violations occur when a subclass overrides a method in a way that weakens preconditions, strengthens postconditions, or throws new exceptions not declared in the parent. LSP is the 'L' in SOLID principles and is the litmus test for whether 'extends' is the right tool for a relationship.

articleHeader.title: Java Inheritance — extends, super, Overriding & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java Inheritance — types of inheritance, extends keyword, super keyword, method overriding, constructor chaining, final keyword, IS-A vs HAS-A, instanceof, Liskov Substitution Principle, anti-patterns, and real-world production code examples.

blocks.text: Inheritance is one of the four pillars of object-oriented programming (alongside Encapsulation, Polymorphism, and Abstraction). It is the mechanism by which one class — called the subclass or child class — acquires the fields and methods of another class — called the superclass or parent class. In Java, inheritance is declared using the extends keyword.

Inheritance models the IS-A relationship between classes. A Dog IS-A Animal. A SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount. A ElectricCar IS-A Vehicle. When this relationship holds, the subclass can reuse the parent's code, extend it with new behaviour, and substitute for the parent wherever the parent type is expected — this is the essence of runtime polymorphism.

The two core benefits of inheritance are: (1) Code Reuse — common logic written once in the parent is inherited by all subclasses without duplication. (2) Polymorphism — a parent type reference can hold any subclass object, and calling a method on it invokes the subclass's version at runtime. This enables writing flexible, extensible systems where new subclasses can be added without modifying existing code.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Inheritance at a Glance
blocks.text: Key facts: (1) Java supports SINGLE inheritance for classes — one class can extend only one parent. (2) Java supports MULTIPLE inheritance through interfaces. (3) Every class in Java implicitly extends java.lang.Object — the root of all class hierarchies. (4) Inherited members include: public and protected fields and methods. private members are NOT inherited — they stay within the declaring class. (5) Constructors are NOT inherited — but the parent constructor is called via super(). (6) Use 'extends' for class inheritance, 'implements' for interface implementation.

The extends keyword is Java's mechanism for declaring that one class inherits from another. It creates a permanent parent-child relationship between the two classes. The subclass automatically receives all non-private members of the superclass and can also define its own additional fields and methods.

items.title: Syntax
What Gets Inherited
items.text:
✅ Inherited: public fields, protected fields, public methods, protected methods, default (package-private) members (same package only).
❌ NOT inherited: private fields and methods (hidden within declaring class), constructors (but accessible via super()), static members (accessible but not 'inherited' in polymorphic sense).

items.title: Single Inheritance Rule
items.text: A Java class can extend ONLY ONE class — this is single inheritance. 'class C extends A, B' is a compile error. This avoids the Diamond Problem. However, a class CAN implement multiple interfaces: 'class C extends A implements B, D'. And an interface CAN extend multiple interfaces: 'interface C extends A, B'.

blocks.text: Java supports several forms of inheritance, each modelling a different structural relationship between classes. Understanding these types helps you design class hierarchies that are clean, logical, and extensible.

items.title: Single Inheritance
items.text: One class extends exactly ONE parent class. The most common and straightforward form. Example: 'class Car extends Vehicle'. Car inherits all accessible members of Vehicle. Java mandates single inheritance to avoid the Diamond Problem. This is the default and most-used inheritance type in Java applications.

items.title: Multilevel Inheritance
items.text: A class extends another class which itself extends another class — forming a chain. Example: Animal → Mammal → Dog. Dog inherits from both Mammal and Animal. The chain can be as long as needed, but deep chains (4+ levels) are generally a code smell — they make the hierarchy fragile and hard to understand. Rule: keep hierarchies shallow.

items.title: Hierarchical Inheritance
items.text: Multiple classes extend the SAME parent class. Example: Vehicle is extended by Car, Truck, and Motorcycle. All three inherit the common Vehicle behaviour but add their own specialisations. This is the most natural use of inheritance — capturing shared structure in a parent and specialising in children.

items.title: Multiple Inheritance — Through Interfaces Only
items.text: Java does NOT allow a class to extend multiple classes. However, a class CAN implement multiple interfaces: 'class Robot implements Movable, Chargeable, Programmable'. And an interface CAN extend multiple interfaces. Java 8+ default methods in interfaces can provide shared implementations, giving most benefits of multiple inheritance without the Diamond Problem.

items.title: Hybrid Inheritance — Not Directly Supported
items.text: A combination of multiple inheritance types. Java does not support hybrid inheritance through classes for the same reason it avoids multiple class inheritance. However, hybrid-like structures are achievable using interfaces and abstract classes together — a common real-world pattern in enterprise frameworks like Spring.

sections.title: The super Keyword — Accessing the Parent

blocks.text: The super keyword in Java is a reference to the immediate parent class. It is the complement to this — where this refers to the current object, super refers to the parent portion of the current object. It has three distinct uses, each critical to working correctly with inheritance.

items.title: super.field — Access Hidden Parent Field
items.text: When a subclass declares a field with the same name as a parent field, the parent's field is 'hidden'. 'super.fieldName' accesses the parent's version. This is rarely needed in well-designed code — field hiding is generally a bad practice. Prefer unique field names in subclasses. But understanding this is essential for exam questions.

items.title: super.method() — Call Overridden Parent Method
items.text: When a subclass overrides a parent method, 'super.method()' calls the parent's original version. This is very common — a subclass often wants to EXTEND rather than REPLACE the parent's behaviour. Example: getDetails() in Car calls 'super.getDetails()' to include the parent's output, then appends its own. Without super, the parent logic must be duplicated.

items.title: super() — Call Parent Constructor
items.text: super(args) calls the parent's constructor. MUST be the FIRST statement in the subclass constructor. If not written explicitly, Java auto-inserts 'super()' (no-arg parent constructor). If the parent has no no-arg constructor, omitting super(args) is a compile error. Used to initialise the inherited portion of the object — the parent's fields need to be set up before the subclass extends them.

double baseSalary, double teamBonus, int teamSize) {
super(name, department, baseSalary); // ✅ Use 1: calls Employee constructor
// ✅ Use 2: call overridden method to extend (not replace) logic
double bonusShare = teamBonus / teamSize;       // Manager's extra
return super.getPaySlip() +  // ✅ Reuse parent's formatted string

blocks.text: When an object is created from a subclass, Java does not just call the subclass constructor. It initiates a constructor chain — walking up the entire inheritance hierarchy and executing each class's constructor from the top (Object) downward. This ensures every level of the hierarchy has a chance to initialise its own fields before the subclass adds to them.

items.title: Constructor Chain Order
items.text:
When 'new GrandChild()' is called, execution order is:
1. GrandChild() starts, immediately calls super()
2. Child() starts, immediately calls super()
3. Object() runs (java.lang.Object constructor)
4. Child() body continues
5. GrandChild() body continues
Each constructor's body runs from TOP (most ancestral) to BOTTOM (most derived). Fields are always initialised before the constructor body they belong to runs.

items.title: The Auto-insert Rule
items.text: If a subclass constructor does NOT explicitly call super() or this() as its first statement, Java automatically inserts 'super()' (no-arg parent constructor) at the very beginning. Consequence: if the parent class has NO no-arg constructor (because a parameterised one was defined), the compile fails with 'no suitable constructor found'. Always explicitly call super(args) when the parent has no default constructor.

items.title: this() vs super() — Cannot Have Both
items.text: Both 'this(args)' (same-class constructor chaining) and 'super(args)' (parent constructor) must be the FIRST statement in a constructor. Therefore, a single constructor CANNOT have both. The way it works: 'this(args)' delegates to another constructor in the same class, which eventually calls super(). The super() call bubbles up through 'this()' chains, not directly.

blocks.text: Method overriding occurs when a subclass provides its own implementation for a method that is already defined in its parent class. It is the mechanism behind runtime polymorphism (dynamic dispatch) — when you call a method on a parent-type reference that actually holds a subclass object, Java calls the subclass's version at runtime, not the parent's.

items.title: Rules for Valid Overriding
items.text:
1. Same method name as parent.
2. Same parameter list (number, types, order).
3. Return type: same, or a covariant (subtype) return.
4. Access modifier: same or WIDER (protected→public ✅, public→protected ❌).
5. Cannot override: private methods (not visible), static methods (hiding, not overriding), final methods.
6. @Override annotation: not mandatory but strongly recommended — compiler catches mistakes.

items.title: Dynamic Dispatch — How Runtime Polymorphism Works
items.text: When 'Animal a = new Dog(); a.makeSound();' is written, Java doesn't decide which makeSound() to call at compile time — it decides at RUNTIME by looking at the actual object type (Dog), not the reference type (Animal). This is dynamic dispatch. The JVM maintains a virtual method table (vtable) for each class — method calls are resolved through this table at runtime. This is how 'write once, work with many types' polymorphism works.

items.title: @Override Annotation
items.text: @Override tells the compiler: 'I intend this to be an override'. The compiler then verifies it actually overrides a parent method. Benefits: (1) Compile error if method name is misspelled. (2) Compile error if parameter list doesn't match. (3) Documents intent clearly. Without @Override, a typo in the method name silently creates a NEW method instead of overriding — a hard-to-find bug.

blocks.title: 💡 Covariant Return Type — Java 5+
blocks.text: An overriding method can return a subtype of the parent's return type. If the parent declares 'Animal create()', the subclass can override with 'Dog create()' — this is valid because Dog IS-A Animal. This is called covariant return type. It allows subclass factory methods to return more specific types without requiring callers to cast. Real example: 'Object.clone()' returns Object, but an overriding clone() can return the specific class type.

sections.title: final with Inheritance — Preventing Extension & Override

blocks.text: The final keyword interacts with inheritance in three important ways — preventing subclassing, preventing method override, and making fields immutable. These restrictions are deliberate design decisions that protect invariants and communicate intent.

rows: Cannot be subclassed — no extends allowed
Security-sensitive or complete implementations: String, Integer, Math
Cannot be overridden in any subclass
Template method pattern — lock core algorithm while allowing hooks
Immutable identity fields: IDs, keys, config values set in constructor
Cannot be reassigned inside the method body
Defensive coding — prevent accidental reassignment of parameters

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A — Choosing Inheritance or Composition

blocks.text: One of the most important design decisions in OOP is choosing between inheritance (IS-A) and composition (HAS-A). Misusing inheritance when composition is appropriate — or vice versa — leads to fragile, unmaintainable class hierarchies. The litmus test is always: does the relationship truly hold in every possible context?

items.title: IS-A — When to Use Inheritance
items.text: Use inheritance when: (1) The subclass genuinely IS a more specific type of the parent — a Dog IS-A Animal, a SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount, an EmailNotification IS-A Notification. (2) The subclass can substitute for the parent in all situations (Liskov Substitution Principle). (3) You want to extend or specialise the parent's behaviour. Red flag: if you need to override a method and throw an exception to say 'not applicable', inheritance is wrong.

items.title: HAS-A — When to Use Composition
items.text: Use composition when: (1) One class CONTAINS or USES another — a Car HAS-A Engine, an Order HAS-A PaymentMethod, a Logger HAS-A Formatter. (2) The relationship is 'uses' or 'is made of', not 'is a type of'. (3) You want flexibility — the 'has-a' component can be swapped at runtime. Composition is more flexible than inheritance — you can change behaviours by injecting different implementations.

items.title: Favour Composition Over Inheritance
items.text: The classic GoF design principle: 'Favour object composition over class inheritance'. Inheritance creates tight coupling — the subclass is intimately coupled to the parent's implementation. Adding a method to the parent can break subclasses. Composition is looser — the outer class only depends on the component's public API. In Spring and modern Java enterprise code, composition (dependency injection) is strongly preferred over deep inheritance trees.

blocks.label: IsAHasADemo.java
lines: // ✅ EmailNotification IS-A Notification — inheritance makes sense
public void start()  { System.out.println(horsePower + "hp engine started."); }
// ✅ Car HAS-A Engine — composition is correct
// ❌ Car extends Engine — WRONG: a Car is NOT a type of Engine
private final Engine  engine;  // HAS-A relationship
this.engine = engine; // Engine injected — can swap petrol/electric
engine.start();  // DELEGATES to the Engine object
// Benefit: engine can be swapped — ElectricEngine, HybridEngine, etc.
// Car car = new Car("Honda", new Engine(150, "Petrol"));
// car.start(); // 150hp engine started. → Honda is now running.

sections.title: instanceof Operator — Type Checking in Inheritance

blocks.text: The instanceof operator tests whether an object is an instance of a specific class, or of a class that inherits from it. It returns true if the object IS-A that type (directly or through inheritance), and false otherwise. Java 16+ enhances this with Pattern Matching instanceof — combining the type check with an automatic cast.

items.title: Classic instanceof
items.text: 'obj instanceof ClassName' — returns true if obj is an instance of ClassName or any of its subclasses. Always returns false for null (never throws NullPointerException). Example: in an inheritance chain Animal → Mammal → Dog, a Dog object is instanceof Dog (true), instanceof Mammal (true), instanceof Animal (true), instanceof Object (true).

items.title: Pattern Matching instanceof (Java 16+)
items.text: 'if (shape instanceof Circle c)' — tests AND casts in one step. If true, 'c' is automatically bound as a Circle reference — no explicit cast needed. The binding variable is in scope only where guaranteed to match. Eliminates the verbose test-then-cast boilerplate. Combined with && for additional conditions: 'if (obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 5)'.

items.title: instanceof in Inheritance Trees
items.text: A subclass object is instanceof its parent, grandparent, and all ancestors — up to Object. 'new Dog() instanceof Animal' → true. 'new Dog() instanceof Object' → true. This is the foundation of polymorphism — you can treat any object through its parent type interface. Use instanceof when you genuinely need to know the specific type; avoid it when polymorphism (method overriding) can handle it more cleanly.

sections.title: java.lang.Object — The Root of All Java Classes

blocks.text: Every class in Java implicitly extends java.lang.Object — even if you don't write extends Object. This means every object, no matter what class it belongs to, inherits a set of core methods from Object. Understanding these methods is essential — some require overriding to work correctly, and their contracts have precise rules.

rows: Any class whose instances will be printed or logged
When two different objects with same data should be 'equal'
Whenever equals() is overridden — always as a pair
When controlled copying is needed — prefer copy constructors
Use try-with-resources or Cleaner API instead

sections.title: Liskov Substitution Principle — The Test of Good Inheritance

blocks.text: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) — the 'L' in SOLID — states: if S is a subtype of T, then objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering the correctness of the program. In plain English: wherever you use a Parent object, you should be able to substitute a Child object and everything should still work correctly.

items.title: LSP-Compliant Inheritance
items.text: A subclass honours the parent's contract: (1) Does not weaken preconditions — accepts at least the same inputs. (2) Does not strengthen postconditions — delivers at least the same guarantees. (3) Does not throw new exceptions not declared by the parent. (4) Preserves invariants — properties that always hold for the parent type. If Dog extends Animal and Animal.makeSound() is supposed to make a non-silent sound, Dog.makeSound() must also make a sound.

items.title: LSP Violations — Classic Example
items.text: The Rectangle-Square problem: Square extends Rectangle seems logical mathematically. But if Rectangle has setWidth() and setHeight() and code sets them independently, Square breaks the contract — setting width also changes height (to stay square), violating the caller's expectation that width and height are independent. The fix: Square should NOT extend Rectangle — they should share a common Shape interface instead.

items.title: How to Detect LSP Violations
items.text: Warning signs: (1) Overriding a method to throw UnsupportedOperationException ('not applicable'). (2) Overriding a method to do nothing (empty body) when the parent's version does something important. (3) Strengthening input validation in an override (rejecting valid parent inputs). (4) Overriding to return null when the parent guarantees non-null. Any of these means inheritance is the wrong tool — use composition or a shared interface instead.

blocks.label: LSPDemo.java
lines: public void setWidth(double w)  { this.width  = w; }
public void setHeight(double h) { this.height = h; }
public double getArea()         { return width * height; }
// ❌ VIOLATES LSP — Square breaks Rectangle's behaviour contract
this.height = w; // Forces equal sides — breaks Rectangle contract!
// Code that works for Rectangle but BREAKS for Square:
// testRectangle(new Square());    // ❌ Fails — area is 9, not 15!
RectangleFixed(double w, double h) { width=w; height=h; }
@Override public double getArea()      { return width * height; }
@Override public double getArea()      { return side * side; }
// Both implement Shape — no LSP violation.
// Square is not forced to pretend it's a mutable Rectangle.
// Contract: always returns a value between 0.0 and 1.0

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Trip Everyone Up

blocks.text: These inheritance-related mistakes appear consistently in Java beginner and intermediate code. Each one either produces a compile-time error or — more dangerously — a silent runtime bug that is difficult to trace.

blocks.label: InheritanceMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Forgetting super() when parent has no no-arg constructor
Vehicle(String brand) { this.brand = brand; } // No default constructor!
// Java auto-inserts super() — but Vehicle has no no-arg constructor!
// ❌ Compile error: no suitable constructor found
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: @Override typo silently creates a NEW method
// Missing @Override — 'makesound' is a NEW method, not an override
public void makesound() { System.out.println("Meow"); } // Silent bug!
// a.makeSound(); // Prints "..." — Cat's method never called!
// ✅ Fix: always add @Override — compiler will catch the typo
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Narrowing access modifier in override
// protected void display() { } // ❌ Compile error — narrows public to protected
public void display() { System.out.println("Derived"); } // ✅ Same or wider
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Calling overridable method from constructor
printInfo(); // ❌ Dangerous — calls overridden version before subclass is ready
// new Child() → NullPointerException in printInfo() before info is set
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: instanceof misused — checking specific type when polymorphism works
// BAD: every time Animal adds a new subclass, this switch breaks
// ✅ Better: use polymorphism — each subclass overrides 'performAction()'

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These inheritance anti-patterns are the most common causes of fragile, unmaintainable class hierarchies in professional Java codebases. Each one has a cleaner alternative.

items.title: Deep Inheritance Chains (The Gorilla-Banana Problem)
items.text: Classes 5+ levels deep — every change to the top of the hierarchy ripples to all descendants. Joe Armstrong (Erlang creator) famously said: 'You wanted a banana but you got a gorilla holding the banana and the entire jungle.' Deep chains are fragile, hard to understand, and signal that composition may be more appropriate. Rule: inheritance hierarchies beyond 3 levels are a code smell.

items.title: Inheriting for Code Reuse Alone
items.text: Using inheritance ONLY because a parent has methods you want — not because a true IS-A relationship exists. Example: 'class Stack extends ArrayList' to reuse ArrayList's storage. But a Stack IS NOT an ArrayList — Stack should restrict access to top only. Result: all ArrayList methods (get(), add(index), remove(index)) are exposed on Stack, breaking encapsulation. Fix: composition — Stack CONTAINS an ArrayList internally.

items.title: Overriding to Disable (UnsupportedOperationException)
items.text: Overriding a method and throwing UnsupportedOperationException to say 'this method doesn't apply here' is a clear LSP violation. If a subclass cannot honour the parent's method contract, the inheritance is wrong. Real example: java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList() adds() throws UnsupportedOperationException — it shouldn't extend a mutable list at all. Fix: use a separate interface or composition.

items.title: Exposing Parent Internals Through Protected Fields
items.text: Making fields 'protected' instead of 'private' because subclasses need them directly is lazy encapsulation. Protected fields tightly couple every subclass to the parent's internal representation. If the parent changes how it stores data, all subclasses break. Fix: keep fields private in the parent and provide protected methods (getters, callbacks) for subclasses to interact with them safely.

items.title: Concrete Class Inheritance Across Libraries
items.text: Extending a concrete class from a third-party library you don't control is risky — the library may add final methods, change behaviour, or the class may not be designed for extension. This creates a tight coupling to an external implementation detail. Fix: wrap the class with composition (Decorator/Adapter pattern). Only extend when the class was explicitly designed for extension.

items.title: Not Overriding equals/hashCode in Value Subclasses
items.text: If a subclass adds fields that are part of equality (e.g., a GoldMember extends Member, adds a 'membershipLevel' field), failing to override equals() and hashCode() in the subclass means two GoldMembers with different levels may compare as equal using the parent's equals(). This breaks Set and Map behaviour. JEP note: Java's Effective Java (Bloch) recommends avoiding extending concrete classes when value equality is involved — use composition.

sections.title: Java Inheritance Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced developer interviews, campus placements, and OCPJP certification exams.

items.q: Q1. What is inheritance in Java and what are its types?
items.a: Inheritance is an OOP mechanism where a subclass acquires fields and methods of a superclass using the 'extends' keyword. It models the IS-A relationship and promotes code reuse and runtime polymorphism. Types in Java: (1) Single — one class extends one parent. (2) Multilevel — A extends B extends C — a chain. (3) Hierarchical — multiple classes extend the same parent. (4) Multiple — NOT supported through classes (Diamond Problem); achieved through interfaces. (5) Hybrid — combination of above, achievable through interfaces. Java mandates single inheritance for classes to avoid ambiguity, but allows multiple interface implementation.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between method overriding and method overloading?
items.a: Overriding: subclass provides a new implementation for a parent's method. SAME name, SAME parameter list, SAME or covariant return type. Resolved at RUNTIME (dynamic dispatch). Requires inheritance. Access modifier can only widen. @Override annotation recommended. Overloading: same class (or inherited) defines multiple methods with the SAME name but DIFFERENT parameter lists. Resolved at COMPILE TIME (static binding). Does not require inheritance. Return type alone cannot differentiate. Memory aid: overrIDing = different at runtIME. Overloading = different at compile time.

items.q: Q3. Why does Java not support multiple inheritance through classes?
items.a: Java avoids the Diamond Problem. If class C extends A and B, and both A and B override a method from their common ancestor, which version does C inherit? This ambiguity makes the language complex and error-prone. Java's solution: (1) Only single inheritance for classes — no ambiguity. (2) Multiple interface implementation allowed — interfaces traditionally had no state and no concrete methods, so no diamond conflict. (3) Java 8 default methods in interfaces can create a similar conflict, resolved by explicit rules: the class's own override wins; if two interfaces provide defaults, the implementing class MUST explicitly override to resolve.

items.q: Q4. What is the super keyword in Java? When must super() be used?
items.a: super refers to the IMMEDIATE parent class and has three uses: (1) super.field — access a parent field hidden by a subclass field with the same name. (2) super.method() — call the parent's version of an overridden method; critical for extending (not replacing) parent behaviour. (3) super(args) — call the parent's constructor; MUST be the first statement in the subclass constructor. super() is auto-inserted if not written — but if the parent has no no-arg constructor, the compile fails. super() and this() cannot both be first statements — super() chains up; this() chains sideways within the same class.

items.q: Q5. Can a subclass override a static method? What is method hiding?
items.a: No — static methods cannot be overridden in the OOP polymorphism sense. If a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a parent's static method, it HIDES the parent's method, not overrides it. The difference: with overriding, the runtime type determines which method runs (dynamic dispatch). With hiding, the REFERENCE type (compile-time type) determines which method runs — the subclass's version runs only when called through a subclass reference. @Override on a static method causes a compile error. Example: 'Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod()' → runs Parent's version. 'Child c = new Child(); c.staticMethod()' → runs Child's version.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A relationships?
items.a: IS-A (inheritance): a subclass IS A more specific type of the parent. Modelled with 'extends'. Example: SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount. Car IS-A Vehicle. Use when the subclass can genuinely substitute for the parent in all situations (Liskov). HAS-A (composition): one class CONTAINS or USES another as a field. Modelled with field declarations. Example: Car HAS-A Engine. Order HAS-A PaymentMethod. Logger HAS-A Formatter. Rule of thumb: 'Favour composition over inheritance' (GoF). Use inheritance for IS-A + LSP compliance. Use composition when you need flexibility to swap components or the relationship is ownership/use rather than type specialisation.

items.q: Q7. What is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?
items.a: LSP states: if S is a subtype of T, objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering correctness. Practical meaning: wherever a Parent reference is used, any Subclass object should work correctly. Violations include: overriding a method to throw UnsupportedOperationException (breaks method contract), narrowing input validation (rejecting inputs the parent accepted), returning null where parent guarantees non-null, or strengthening postconditions. Classic violation: Square extending Rectangle — setting width also changes height, breaking code that expects independent width/height. Fix: make them sibling implementations of a Shape interface instead of one extending the other.

items.q: Q8. What happens when a constructor is called in an inheritance chain?
items.a: Java initiates a constructor chain from most derived to most ancestral, but executes from most ancestral to most derived. When 'new C()' is called (where C extends B extends A): C() starts → auto-calls super() → B() starts → auto-calls super() → A() starts → Object() runs → A() body continues → B() body continues → C() body continues. Each constructor's body runs after all parent constructors complete. This ensures parent fields are initialised before the child tries to build on top of them. If the parent has no no-arg constructor and the child doesn't explicitly call super(args), it's a compile error.

items.q: Q9. Can we override the equals() method in a subclass that extends a class already overriding equals()?
items.a: Yes, you can, but it is tricky and generally advised against for concrete subclasses (Effective Java Item 10). The issue: if Parent overrides equals() based on certain fields, and Child adds new fields, Child's equals() that considers those extra fields can break the symmetry contract of equals(). Example: Parent.equals(Child) might return true but Child.equals(Parent) returns false — symmetry violated. The recommended approach: if you add fields that affect equality, use composition instead of inheritance, or mark Parent as abstract so the subclass always defines equals completely. Java records (Java 16+) provide automatic, correct equals/hashCode based on all components.

items.q: Q10. What is the output of: 'Animal a = new Dog(); a.makeSound();' if both Animal and Dog define makeSound()?
items.a: Dog's makeSound() is called — this is RUNTIME POLYMORPHISM (dynamic dispatch). The reference type is Animal, but the actual object at runtime is a Dog. Java uses the vtable (virtual method table) to look up the actual runtime type and call that type's method. This is the core power of inheritance + overriding — you can write code that works against the parent type (Animal) but executes the most specific subclass behaviour at runtime. This is why frameworks like Spring can call methods on proxy objects, why Collections.sort() works for any Comparable, and why plugin systems work.

items.a: Output: A  B  C. When 'new C()' is called: C() constructor starts, auto-inserts super() which calls B(). B() starts, auto-inserts super() which calls A(). A() starts, prints 'A', returns. B() body resumes, prints 'B', returns. C() body resumes, prints 'C'. Constructors always execute from most ancestral (top) to most derived (bottom). This is the constructor chain — it ensures every level initialises itself before the child extends it.

COMPILE ERROR. Animal defines only a parameterised constructor 'Animal(String name)' — this removes the automatic default no-arg constructor. Dog's constructor 'Dog()' doesn't explicitly call super(), so Java auto-inserts 'super()'. But 'super()' (no-arg) doesn't exist in Animal — compile error: 'no suitable constructor found in class Animal'. Fix: 'Dog() { super("Unknown"); System.out.println("Dog created"); }' — explicitly call the available constructor.

Output: 'Child: Child'  then  'Parent'. display() is an instance method — dynamic dispatch applies. 'p' holds a Child object, so Child.display() runs, printing 'Child: Child'. For field access ('p.name'), fields are NOT polymorphic — they are resolved based on the REFERENCE TYPE at compile time, not the runtime object type. Since 'p' is declared as type Parent, 'p.name' resolves to Parent's 'name' field = 'Parent'. Key rule: method calls are polymorphic (runtime type); field access is NOT (reference type). This is why fields should always be private.

items.q: 4. Design a class hierarchy for a Shape system: Shape (abstract, getArea(), getPerimeter()), Circle, Rectangle, and Square. Square should use composition or correct inheritance. Add a ShapeCalculator that works with any Shape.
items.a: abstract class Shape { public abstract double getArea(); public abstract double getPerimeter(); public String describe() { return String.format("%s | Area: %.2f | Perimeter: %.2f", getClass().getSimpleName(), getArea(), getPerimeter()); } }  class Circle extends Shape { private final double radius; Circle(double r) { if(r<=0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); this.radius=r; } @Override public double getArea() { return Math.PI*radius*radius; } @Override public double getPerimeter() { return 2*Math.PI*radius; } }  class Rectangle extends Shape { protected final double width, height; Rectangle(double w, double h) { if(w<=0||h<=0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); this.width=w; this.height=h; } @Override public double getArea() { return width*height; } @Override public double getPerimeter() { return 2*(width+height); } }  class Square extends Shape { private final double side; Square(double s) { if(s<=0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); this.side=s; } @Override public double getArea() { return side*side; } @Override public double getPerimeter() { return 4*side; } }  // Square does NOT extend Rectangle — LSP would be violated. class ShapeCalculator { public double totalArea(List<Shape> shapes) { return shapes.stream().mapToDouble(Shape::getArea).sum(); } }

LSP Violation: code that expects any Bird to fly() will break with a Penguin. 'Bird b = new Penguin(); b.fly();' throws UnsupportedOperationException — the parent's contract is broken. Penguin CANNOT substitute for Bird when flying is involved. Fix: Restructure the hierarchy. Introduce a Flyable interface: 'interface Flyable { void fly(); }'. Make Bird abstract or concrete but without fly(). Only birds that actually fly implement Flyable: 'class Sparrow extends Bird implements Flyable'. 'class Penguin extends Bird' (no Flyable). Now 'Flyable f = new Penguin()' is a compile error — the type system prevents the violation.

Output: 'Base static'  then  'Derived instance'. staticMethod(): static methods are NOT overridden — they are HIDDEN. Method hiding is resolved at compile time based on the REFERENCE TYPE. 'obj' is declared as Base, so Base.staticMethod() runs — printing 'Base static'. instanceMethod(): instance methods ARE overridden — dynamic dispatch applies. The runtime type of 'obj' is Derived, so Derived.instanceMethod() runs — printing 'Derived instance'. Key: static = compile-time resolution (reference type). Instance = runtime resolution (actual object type).

items.q: 7. Write a multilevel inheritance example: LivingBeing → Animal → Pet → Dog. Each class adds one field and one method. Show constructor chaining.
items.a: class LivingBeing { boolean alive; LivingBeing(boolean alive) { this.alive=alive; System.out.println("LivingBeing()"); } void breathe() { System.out.println("Breathing..."); } }  class Animal extends LivingBeing { String species; Animal(String species) { super(true); this.species=species; System.out.println("Animal()"); } void makeSound() { System.out.println(species+" makes a sound."); } }  class Pet extends Animal { String ownerName; Pet(String species, String owner) { super(species); this.ownerName=owner; System.out.println("Pet()"); } void greetOwner() { System.out.println("Greeting "+ownerName+"!"); } }  class Dog extends Pet { String breed; Dog(String owner, String breed) { super("Canis lupus", owner); this.breed=breed; System.out.println("Dog()"); } void fetch() { System.out.println(breed+" fetches the ball!"); } }  // new Dog("Ravi","Labrador") prints: LivingBeing() → Animal() → Pet() → Dog() // Dog object can call: breathe(), makeSound(), greetOwner(), fetch()

items.q: 8. Explain why 'class Stack extends ArrayList' is a bad design. What is the correct approach?
items.a: Stack extends ArrayList violates the IS-A principle and LSP. A Stack IS NOT a general-purpose ArrayList — a Stack should only allow push, pop, and peek (top only). But by extending ArrayList, Stack inherits all ArrayList operations: get(index), add(index, elem), remove(index), addAll() — allowing direct access at any position. This defeats the purpose of a stack (LIFO only). LSP violation: code expecting any List can break the stack's LIFO contract. Example: ArrayList<T> list = new Stack<T>(); list.add(0, item); // bypasses LIFO — inserts at bottom! Correct design: Stack CONTAINS a List (composition). 'public class Stack<T> { private final Deque<T> storage = new ArrayDeque<>(); public void push(T item) { storage.push(item); } public T pop() { return storage.pop(); } public T peek() { return storage.peek(); } public boolean isEmpty() { return storage.isEmpty(); } } — Only LIFO operations exposed. Internal storage hidden. (Note: java.util.Stack itself has this problem in the JDK — Deque/ArrayDeque is preferred.)

blocks.text: Inheritance is one of Java's most powerful features — and one of the most frequently misused. When used correctly, it enables clean code reuse, elegant polymorphism, and extensible architectures. When misused — for code reuse without a true IS-A relationship, or in violation of LSP — it creates fragile, tightly-coupled hierarchies that are painful to maintain.

The professional's approach: always ask the IS-A question first. Does this relationship hold in every context, without exception? Does the subclass honour the parent's contract completely? Can I substitute the child wherever the parent is expected? If yes to all — inheritance is right. If no — composition is likely the better tool. The Template Method, Decorator, Strategy, and Composite patterns often provide better design alternatives than deep inheritance trees.

items.q: What is inheritance in Java?
items.a: Inheritance in Java is an OOP mechanism where one class (subclass/child) acquires the fields and methods of another class (superclass/parent) using the 'extends' keyword. It models the IS-A relationship — a Dog IS-A Animal, a SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount. Java supports single inheritance for classes (one direct parent) to avoid the Diamond Problem, but allows multiple interface implementation. Every class implicitly extends java.lang.Object.

items.q: What is the difference between method overriding and method overloading?
items.a: Method Overriding: subclass provides a new implementation for a parent's method with the SAME name and SAME parameter list. Resolved at RUNTIME (dynamic dispatch). Requires inheritance. Access modifier can only widen. Method Overloading: same class defines multiple methods with the SAME name but DIFFERENT parameter lists. Resolved at COMPILE TIME. Does not require inheritance. Return type alone cannot differentiate overloaded methods.

items.q: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance through classes?
items.a: Java avoids the Diamond Problem — if C extends A and B, and both A and B have different overrides of the same method, which version does C inherit? This ambiguity makes programs complex and error-prone. Java's solution: single inheritance for classes; multiple interface implementation for type flexibility. Java 8+ default methods in interfaces can create similar conflicts, resolved by explicit override rules in the implementing class.

items.q: What is the super keyword in Java?
items.a: The 'super' keyword refers to the immediate parent class. Three uses: (1) super.field — access a parent field hidden by a same-name subclass field. (2) super.method() — call the parent's version of an overridden method to extend (not replace) parent behaviour. (3) super(args) — call the parent constructor from a subclass constructor; must be the very first statement. If omitted, Java auto-inserts super(), requiring the parent to have a no-arg constructor.

items.q: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?
items.a: LSP states that objects of a subclass must be substitutable for objects of the parent class without breaking program correctness. In practice: a subclass must honour the parent's method contracts — same input acceptance, same output guarantees, no new exceptions. Violations include overriding to throw UnsupportedOperationException or to do nothing when the parent's behaviour was meaningful. Classic violation: Square extending Rectangle — setting width changes height, breaking independent dimension expectations.
